analysis.title: Uncommon truths: Focus on the economy, not the politics
key_insights: The US mid-terms produced a larger than expected swing to the Democrats. As of 7 November they lead 254 vs 162 in the House (a majority of 80-90 seats) and 54 vs 44 in the Senate, against pre-election Republican majorities of 3 and 6. The swing is not excessive versus historical mid-term precedents.

Congressional ability to legislate is limited. Overriding a presidential veto needs two thirds of both houses (67 Senate votes, 290 House votes), so the president keeps an effective veto unless Republicans break ranks.
Some Republicans may break ranks with the president on the war with Iran, which has damaged their standing. If the president yields, that could mean lower energy costs, inflation and bond yields.

Republican support for greater AI and datacentre regulation is likely harder to get, so the post-election sell-off in global technology stocks may have been overdone. Real regulatory risk may wait for the next presidential election if a Democrat wins.
Tech weakness predates the mid-terms. As of 30 October US hyperscalers were largely flat year-to-date and US neocloud stocks had halved since mid-year, as markets worried AI was overpriced.

Since 1990 US asset returns have tended to be better in the year after mid-term elections than in the election year. 2006, 2010 and 2014 were exceptions. This is some comfort for fixed income investors after a tough 2026.

Economic data remain reassuring. Q3 GDP grew 3.4% annualised despite a 3.3% drag from net exports. ISM Manufacturing rose to 55.5 in October from 54.5, and ISM Services fell to 54.5 from 54.9. Auto sales and construction spending were weak.

Labour data are solid. JOLTS openings rose to 7.5 million in September from 7.1 million and layoffs declined. Challenger job cuts stayed low and initial jobless claims were near five-year lows. October payrolls rose 165k with an 84k upward revision to the prior two months, and unemployment fell to 4.1% from 4.2%.

Wage growth was 3.1% versus a Bloomberg consensus of 2.9%, but it was down from the prior month. Falling unemployment since last November has not raised wage growth. Strong productivity pushed Q3 unit labour cost growth negative.

The Fed may feel the need to tighten again to prevent second round effects from higher food and energy prices, but the November University of Michigan survey shows consumer inflation expectations easing.
The author expects a resilient economy to keep profits growing and the Fed to tighten less than feared, which should outweigh any mid-term effect in 2027 and support another good year for small caps.

In the week to 6 November, MSCI World fell 2.7% (US -2.8%, Japan -7.5%, EM -4.1%) while China rose 5.4% and Europe was flat at +0.1%. Global technology was the weakest sector at -4.6% relative on the week and -13.0% over the month.
The US 10-year yield was 4.86% and GSCI Energy fell 11.2% on the week but is up 118.8% year-to-date.

Model asset allocation is underweight bonds (34% vs 40% neutral) and overweight equities (50% vs 45% neutral). The equity allocation changes were a cut to Europe ex-UK and Japan, and India was added to the portfolio.

sector_views.rationale: A resilient economy and growing profits should make 2027 another good year for small caps.
The post-election sell-off in global tech may have been overdone, but problems started before the mid-terms and markets feared AI was overpriced.

The Fed may tighten again to prevent second round effects from higher food and energy prices.
Weak auto sales and construction spending.

vol_and_positioning: Momentum was the weakest US factor, at -7.5% on the week and -13.8% on the month. Low volatility (+7.1% over the month), quality (+7.0%), size (+8.5%) and value (+6.6%) all outperformed on the month.
The US equal-weighted market (-1.0% on the week) outperformed the cap-weighted S&P 500 (-2.7%) over the week.
geopolitical: The war with Iran has damaged Republican standing, and some Republicans may break ranks with the president over it.
Higher food and energy prices are a risk of second round inflation effects.

tension_points.bull_case: Asset returns since 1990 have tended to be better in the year after mid-terms. A resilient economy, growing profits and a Fed that tightens less than feared should outweigh mid-term effects in 2027 and support small caps.
tension_points.bear_case: Markets were already worried about overpriced AI, hyperscalers were flat year-to-date and neoclouds had halved. The Fed may need to tighten again over food and energy prices. The 2006, 2010 and 2014 mid-term cycles were exceptions to the pattern.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The Fed tightening more than feared, or the economy losing its current resilience.

theme_stances.key_argument: Congress has limited ability to make big changes, and reassuring economic data and Fed policy matter more for markets.
theme_stances.evidence: prefer to focus on economic data which remains reassuring
